prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B019 as a single-achievement prize, but with a narrower citation and less confidence than in round 1. The core is unchanged: Bistritzer and MacDonald gave a quantitative, testable prediction of where flat bands appear, Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle, and many independent groups using transport, scanning tunnelling and spectroscopy have since reproduced the phase diagram. That is the prediction-then-surprise structure I trust. It has also produced a general platform (twisted TMDs, fractional Chern insulators) rather than a single result. Four colleagues prefer B042 and I take that seriously as a statement that the clock case is settled, but a support count is not a scientific argument, and the question I have to answer for myself is whether the discovery of the phases is robust enough to honour now. I think it is, provided the citation says nothing about the pairing mechanism or the nature of the correlated states. The citation I propose rewards only what has been repeatedly observed: the flat bands and the existence of the correlated and superconducting phases.
statement.case_against: Maturity and credit remain the real weaknesses. Eight years is short, the superconducting pairing mechanism and several correlated states are unresolved, and twist-angle and strain disorder still make sample-to-sample comparison difficult. On credit, Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, the early experimental groups (Dean, Kim, Young, Efetov, Ashoori) and the earlier twist-angle continuum work of Lopes dos Santos and collaborators cannot all be met within three names. A citation worded around the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero discovery handles the theory side reasonably well but does not remove the experimental credit problem, only records it. If a majority concludes that the field is too young, B042 is the better-settled discovery and I would support Katori and Ye without reluctance. I would not describe that as a poor outcome, only a different judgement about timing.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the committee gains anything by waiting a few years on twisted bilayers when the lattice-clock case is already complete, and notes that the object honoured in B019 is a set of phases whose origin is still argued.
responses.response: That is the strongest argument against my position and I do not think it can be dismissed. My answer is that what we would reward is the observation, not the explanation: the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle is established by many groups, and a narrow citation would not be undermined if the mechanism turns out to be, say, phonon-assisted or purely electronic. The risk of waiting is not that the discovery goes away but that the credit becomes harder to assign as the field grows. Where I concede ground is on the Ye side of B042: your suggestion that Ye's role be worded as realisation at record accuracy, not as comb work, answers my round-1 question about separation from 2005, and I now regard the lattice-clock citation as defensible.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B042 and notes that B019 is attractive as prediction plus experiment but has an open superconductivity mechanism; he asks whether to wait, and lists B019 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the open mechanism is the right thing to be cautious about, and I appreciate that you hold B019 as your first fall-back. I would separate two timing questions that the discussion tends to run together. For the clock, you ask whether to wait for the redefinition of the second. I agree with you and Kroll that this is a metrological decision and should not enter the citation, so it is not a reason to wait. For twisted bilayers, the equivalent point is that the mechanism need not be settled for the observed phases to be prize-worthy. If we apply the same standard to both, namely robustly reproduced observation without claims about explanation, both pass. The remaining difference between us is then one of kind, a new state of matter versus a record-setting instrument, and that is a matter of judgement, not of evidence.

responses.point: Mehlig says the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model magic angle is the central idea, but that the earlier numerical twist-angle work of Lopes dos Santos and collaborators is a genuine priority question and the mechanism is a bigger open issue than I suggested.
responses.response: I accept both points. On priority, the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto work established the moire band reconstruction and low-energy flat-band tendency at small angles, but the quantitative magic-angle prediction that told experimenters where to look, and the explanation in terms of a vanishing Fermi velocity, is Bistritzer and MacDonald's. I would handle this through the citation wording on the flat-band magic angle prediction, and I would record the earlier work in the committee's background document, not displace a name. I also agree the mechanism is more open than my round-1 text suggested, which is why I have tightened the citation so that it says nothing about pairing. I cannot verify the finer history from the files, and that remains an uncertainty.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B032 for IceCube, argues the diffuse flux is secure, and says he would not oppose B019 but would want more years of settled interpretation before placing it above an observational discovery.
responses.response: I respect the argument that a new messenger is a discovery of nature in the plainest sense, and the diffuse flux does look secure across several channels. My difficulty is outside my expertise but worth stating: the attribution you describe leaves out AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leaders, and individual sources are at 3-4 sigma, so the citation would also have to avoid saying where the neutrinos come from, which is the interesting question. That seems to me structurally similar to the twisted-bilayer situation, a secure observation with an open explanation. If we accept that for IceCube, I do not see why we cannot for B019. I defer to you and Pearce on the astroparticle credit itself and would not rank B032 above B019 or B042 on what I know.

responses.point: Olsson, who also prefers B019, says the experimental credit is clean only at the level of group leadership, that the first author and student team cannot be named, and that B042 is the cleaner and more mature alternative.
responses.response: I agree and think the committee should state plainly in its background material that Cao and the early experimental teams are acknowledged but cannot be named under the three-person rule. I also agree that B042 is the cleaner and more mature case, which is why I keep it as my first alternative. Where I remain slightly more willing than you is on timing: eight years with wide reproduction is comparable to several past condensed-matter prizes, and I would not wait only for the mechanism. Your point that the original experiment can be pointed to, and not a later and more elegant one, is the criterion I would use to defend the Jarillo-Herrero credit.

uncertainties: Whether eight years is enough to separate robust phenomenology from the unsettled pairing mechanism, and whether the committee will accept that the citation can be silent on mechanism.
Whether the omission of Yuan Cao and the early experimental groups can be handled in the citation and background document alone; my recollection of the history is not independently verified.
Whether the earlier Lopes dos Santos twist-angle theory should change the credited theory names or only the wording.
Whether lattice-clock priority beyond Katori and Ye (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and others) would change the B042 pair; I defer to the atomic physicists and cannot assess it myself.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the credited people on B019, B042 or B058. My work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism is adjacent to the moire materials field, which could bias me toward B019, and I defer to colleagues on atomic clocks and on the astroparticle and particle candidates. My disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
